claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is primarily governed by kinetic arrest from sluggish nanoscale diffusion.
High configurational entropy alone does not govern stability in high-entropy nanoalloys.
The comparison begins with disordered, single-phase, multi-principal-element nanoparticles at room temperature.
Particle size can be varied while composition and synthesis protocol are held constant.
Annealing at approximately 900 degrees Celsius activates atomic mobility without introducing extrinsic effects when performed under an inert atmosphere.
Nanoparticle size affects effective diffusion length and diffusion kinetics.
Smaller nanoparticles have a higher surface-to-volume ratio than larger nanoparticles.
The higher surface-to-volume ratio of smaller particles produces enhanced kinetic hindrance.
Reduced atomic mobility in smaller nanoparticles limits rearrangements that would cause phase separation or chemical segregation.
Larger nanoparticles are closer to bulk behavior and permit more atomic diffusion than smaller nanoparticles.
Greater atomic diffusion makes larger nanoparticles more susceptible to thermodynamically driven phase transformations.
After high-temperature annealing, smaller nanoparticles will retain a disordered single-phase structure with minimal chemical segregation.
After the same anneal, larger nanoparticles will show more phase separation or chemical inhomogeneity than smaller nanoparticles.
Intermediate-size nanoparticles or bulk analogs have less hindered diffusion and express thermodynamic drivers for phase separation more fully.
The prediction is intended to apply to comparisons of particles around 10 nm with particles around 30–50 nm under diffusion-activating thermal conditions.
The size and temperature thresholds at which kinetic effects dominate may depend on alloy composition and processing conditions.
XRD, TEM, and EDX can be used to compare phase uniformity and chemical homogeneity after annealing.
A lack of significant size-dependent difference in phase uniformity or segregation would falsify the proposed size-dependent kinetic-hindrance hypothesis.
